lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.title: Concept model B: identity theft and cybersecurity

objective: Learners analyze three fictional contact attempts, a phishing email, a fake tech-support call, and a legitimate bank mailing, identify the specific red flags in each, and build a three-step personal response plan for any future request for financial or account information.
scenario: This task never asks the learner for any real account, password, or personal information. Every contact attempt described below is fictional and constructed for practice only.
safetyNotes: This task teaches recognition of identity-theft attempts; it never collects any real credential from the learner.
If a learner has received a real message like any of these, the correct response is to show a trusted adult immediately, not to reply.
materials: the three fictional contact attempts on this task sheet

tasks.directions: Read fictional Contact 1, an email: 'URGENT: Your account will be suspended in 1 hour. Click here and enter your username and password immediately to verify your identity.'

prompts.text: Is Contact 1 legitimate or a phishing attempt?
Name at least two specific red flags in Contact 1's wording.

tasks.directions: Read fictional Contact 2, a phone call: 'This is tech support. We detected a virus on your account. Please read us the verification code that was just texted to your phone so we can fix it.'

prompts.text: Is Contact 2 legitimate or a scam attempt?
Explain why a real verification code should never be read aloud to someone who called you, even if they say they are tech support.

tasks.directions: Read fictional Contact 3, a paper letter mailed to the house: 'Your monthly statement is enclosed. No action is needed unless you have a question, in which case call the number printed on the back of your own card.'

prompts.text: Is Contact 3 legitimate or a scam attempt?
Name the specific feature of Contact 3 that makes it safer than Contacts 1 and 2 (hint: who controls the phone number used to respond).

tasks.directions: Build your own three-step response plan.

prompts.text: Write a three-step plan for what you will do if you ever receive a message or call asking you to verify an account by giving a password, code, or card number: step 1, step 2, step 3.

remediation: If a learner marks the legitimate mailed statement as a scam, or misses a red flag in the phishing email, reteach with a two-column red-flag reference sheet (urgency language, a request for a code or password, an unfamiliar link or caller-provided phone number) and have the learner check each of the three contacts against the sheet line by line.
extension: Have the learner research, with an adult, one real published example of a common phishing or scam technique and explain, in writing, which of this lesson's red flags it used.
